claims.claim: EPA's non-hazardous materials and waste management hierarchy ranks options from most to least preferred: (1) source reduction and reuse, (2) recycling and composting, (3) energy recovery, (4) treatment and disposal, with source reduction as the most environmentally preferred strategy.
The United States generated 292.4 million tons of municipal solid waste in 2018, about 4.9 pounds per person per day.
Of 2018 U.S. MSW, about 50 percent (more than 146 million tons) was landfilled, 32.1 percent was recycled and composted, and 11.8 percent (nearly 35 million tons) was combusted with energy recovery.
By share of 2018 MSW generation, the largest categories were paper and paperboard (23.1%), food (21.6%), plastics (12.2%), and yard trimmings (12.1%).
Landfill gas is roughly 50 percent methane and 50 percent carbon dioxide, produced when microbes decompose organic waste under anaerobic (oxygen-free) conditions.
Municipal solid waste landfills were the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions in the United States, accounting for about 14.4 percent in 2022.
Source reduction is ranked highest because preventing waste before it is created reduces emissions, conserves natural resources and energy, reduces the toxicity of waste, and saves money.
Wasted food sent to landfills generates methane, which is why EPA's Wasted Food Scale places landfilling and incineration among the least preferred pathways and prevention at the top.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How current are the national MSW totals?
positions: EPA's Advancing Sustainable Materials Management: Facts and Figures series reports 2018 as its most recent data year.
Newer methane-emission figures (2022) come from EPA's Greenhouse Gas Inventory / LMOP, a separate dataset.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Present MSW tonnage/composition as 2018 EPA Facts and Figures data and the methane share as 2022 inventory data, dating each explicitly so the two are not confused.
